draft.title: Types of penalties
card: Fine
The offender pays money to the state. It is used for less serious offences.
Good behaviour bond
The offender is released on a promise to obey the law for a set time. If they break it, they can be brought back to court and sentenced again.
Community-based orders

A community correction order lets the offender live in the community under court conditions, such as supervision or unpaid work. An intensive correction order is a prison sentence of up to two years served in the community under strict conditions.
Imprisonment
The offender is held in custody. It is the most serious penalty and is used for serious offences.
draft.remember: Penalties run from paying money, through supervision in the community, to custody in prison.

a.q: Which penalty is a prison sentence that the offender serves in the community under strict conditions?
opts: Intensive correction order
Community correction order
Good behaviour bond
Fine
a.why: An intensive correction order replaces a short prison term with close supervision in the community. A community correction order is tempting, but it is not a prison sentence served outside prison. It sets court conditions without a custodial term.
a.clue: Look for the order that is a prison term served outside prison.

b.q: Dev is convicted of a minor offence. The court releases him without a penalty now, on a promise to obey the law for 12 months. What happens if he reoffends in that time?
opts: He can be brought back to court and sentenced again
He must pay a fine to the state straight away
He is automatically placed in prison for 12 months
He must start unpaid work under supervision
b.why: This is a good behaviour bond. The bond is a promise backed by the chance of being sentenced again if it is broken. A fine and unpaid work are different penalties, and a bond does not automatically lead to prison.
b.clue: Think about what gives a promise to obey the law its force.

b.best: He can be brought back to court and sentenced again

problems.detail: The good behaviour bond is out of date in NSW. Since the 2018 sentencing reforms (in force 24 September 2018), good behaviour bonds have been replaced by conditional release orders and community correction orders. The card should name the current order, or at least note that the 2009 syllabus term has been replaced.

The question and its why describe a good behaviour bond, which no longer exists in NSW. Today Dev would receive a conditional release order. The answer logic still holds, but the penalty named is out of date.

An ICO is described as 'up to two years'. That is the limit for a single offence; for an aggregate sentence covering several offences it can be up to three years. The card states the two-year limit without that qualification.
The right option is the only one with a hedge ('can'). Every distractor is absolute ('automatically', 'must'), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

proposal.title: Types of penalties
card: Fine
The offender pays money to the state. It is mostly used for less serious offences.
Conditional release order
Since 2018 this has replaced the good behaviour bond in NSW. The offender is released on conditions, such as being of good behaviour, and a breach can lead to being resentenced.
Community correction order
The offender lives in the community under court conditions, such as supervision or unpaid work, for up to three years.
Prison sentences

An intensive correction order (ICO) is a prison term served in the community under strict conditions, up to two years for one offence or three for several. Full-time imprisonment is the most serious penalty.
proposal.remember: Penalties run from paying money, through orders served in the community, to full-time custody.

a.q: Which penalty is a prison sentence that the offender serves in the community under strict conditions?
opts: Intensive correction order
Community correction order
Conditional release order
Fine
a.why: An intensive correction order is a prison term that is served in the community rather than in jail. A community correction order is tempting, as it also has conditions, but it is not a prison sentence.
a.clue: Look for the order that counts as a prison term.

b.q: Dev is given a conditional release order for a minor offence. Months later, while still on the order, he reoffends. What can the court do about the first offence?
opts: Resentence him for the original offence
Nothing, because the order carries no penalty
Deal with the new offence only, not the old one
Drop the new charge since he is already on an order
b.why: Breaching a conditional release order can lead to Dev being resentenced for the original offence. That chance is what gives the order its force. It is wrong to think the order carries no consequence just because no penalty was imposed at first.
b.clue: Think about what gives the conditions of the order their force.

b.best: Resentence him for the original offence
